find: Heat treatment processes are most commonly applied to carbon steels and high-speed steels. They are generally not used for mild steel (too little carbon to respond significantly) and cannot make non-ferrous metals such as aluminium hard in the same way, though aluminium alloys can be heat-treated to improve strength by a different mechanism (precipitation hardening).
replace: Hardening and tempering are most commonly applied to medium and high carbon steels and to high-speed steels. They do not work on mild steel, which holds too little carbon to respond. Mild steel can still be annealed, normalised or case hardened. Hardening also cannot make non-ferrous metals such as aluminium hard in the same way, though aluminium alloys can be heat-treated to improve strength by a different mechanism (precipitation hardening).
note: F4: the lesson elsewhere anneals and case hardens mild steel; only hardening and tempering fail on it.

find: • Reclaim — recover material that would otherwise be wasted. Swarf and off-cuts from machining operations are collected and returned to smelters. Precious metals such as gold and silver are recovered from waste electronic equipment (e-waste) through urban mining.
replace: • Refuse — say no to a material, a part or a product that is not needed. A designer can refuse a metal with a damaging supply chain, or refuse decorative parts that add mass, cost and waste. A buyer can refuse a product that cannot be repaired or recycled at the end of its life.
note: F1: Refuse is the sixth R on this spec; Reclaim is not taught here.

expect:
Students may include:
Reduce: design the gate using less steel (e.g. hollow tube section rather than solid bar) to reduce embodied energy without compromising structural performance.
Reuse: if the gate is removed during renovation, it can be sold or donated for reuse at another property, avoiding the energy cost of remanufacture.
Recycle: at end of life, the steel can be 100% recycled; recycled steel uses approximately 74% less energy than virgin steel, significantly reducing lifecycle carbon.
Reclaim: steel swarf from machining gate components is reclaimed by the fabricator and returned to a scrap dealer or smelter.
Repair: rather than replacing a corroded gate, sandblasting and re-painting or re-galvanising extends its life, deferring replacement and the associated resource consumption.
Rethink: designing the gate without mixed-material components (e.g. plastic decorative elements bonded to steel) makes end-of-life recycling easier and more effective.
[6 marks — Mastering: At least four of the 6Rs applied specifically to the steel gate with developed environmental impact explanation. Secure: Three Rs applied with some development. Developing: Two Rs listed with limited development; little link to environmental impact. Emerging: Vague mention of recycling without development.]
value:
Students may include:
Reduce: design the gate using less steel (e.g. hollow tube section rather than solid bar) to reduce embodied energy without compromising structural performance.
Reuse: if the gate is removed during renovation, it can be sold or donated for reuse at another property, avoiding the energy cost of remanufacture.
Recycle: at end of life, the steel can be 100% recycled; recycled steel uses approximately 74% less energy than virgin steel, significantly reducing lifecycle carbon.
Refuse: reject an over-specified design or an unnecessary part; for example, refuse decorative cast panels that add steel and weight for no functional gain.
Repair: rather than replacing a corroded gate, sandblasting and re-painting or re-galvanising extends its life, deferring replacement and the associated resource consumption.
Rethink: designing the gate without mixed-material components (e.g. plastic decorative elements bonded to steel) makes end-of-life recycling easier and more effective.
[6 marks — Mastering: At least four of the 6Rs applied specifically to the steel gate with developed environmental impact explanation. Secure: Three Rs applied with some development. Developing: Two Rs listed with limited development; little link to environmental impact. Emerging: Vague mention of recycling without development.]
note: F1: the mark scheme credited Reclaim, which is not one of the six Rs on this spec.
